page_contents_html:
Vaginal infections — not STIs

This pathway covers the assessment and management of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age, focusing on bacterial vaginosis (BV) and vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush) — the two most common non-STI causes of vaginal discharge.

Abnormal vaginal discharge is one of the most common presentations in primary care. Causes include:

  • Physiological — normal variation; increased around ovulation, pregnancy, or with hormonal contraception
  • Bacterial vaginosis — most common cause (~40% of symptomatic cases); overgrowth of anaerobes with reduction of normal lactobacilli
  • Vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush) — second most common (~20–25%); Candida albicans in ~90% of cases
  • Sexually transmitted infections — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomonas (~10–15%); must be excluded in high-risk women
  • Other — foreign body, atrophic vaginitis, cervical pathology, desquamative inflammatory vaginitis

STI exclusion is essential before attributing symptoms to BV or candidiasis in women with any risk factors for STIs. Syndromic treatment without STI testing is only appropriate in clearly low-risk women with characteristic symptoms.

This pathway covers women of reproductive age presenting to primary care. For post-menopausal women with new discharge, see referral criteria below.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Assess all women presenting with vaginal discharge using a structured approach.

History

  • Nature of discharge: colour, consistency, volume, odour
  • Associated symptoms: itch, soreness, dysuria (external), dyspareunia, vulval inflammation or fissuring
  • Cyclical pattern (candidiasis often pre-menstrual)
  • Worse after intercourse or menstruation (BV often worse after sex)
  • Upper reproductive tract symptoms: pelvic/abdominal pain, fever, deep dyspareunia, intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding — if present, consider PID
  • Treatments already tried (OTC antifungals, antibiotics)
  • Past history of BV or candidiasis; previous STIs
  • Pregnancy status

STI risk stratification

Classify before deciding investigation vs empirical treatment.

High STI risk — investigate; do not treat empirically

  • Age <25
  • Previous STI
  • New sexual partner in last 12 months, or >1 partner in last 12 months
  • Partner with known or suspected STI
  • Upper reproductive tract symptoms (pelvic pain, fever, deep dyspareunia)
  • Bloody or blood-stained discharge
  • Uncertain or atypical symptoms
  • Pregnant, post-partum, post-TOP, or post-uterine instrumentation
  • Recurrent symptoms or previous failed treatment

Any one criterion is sufficient to classify as high risk. Examine and investigate — see below.

Lower STI risk — syndromic management appropriate

  • None of the high-risk criteria above
  • Symptoms are characteristic of BV or candidiasis (see differential below)
  • Woman has been in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship

Syndromic treatment is appropriate; examination is not always required but should be considered if diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are not resolving.

Examination and investigations

Lower STI risk with characteristic symptoms: Examination is not always required. Speculum may be omitted in a young woman never sexually active. Examination warranted if diagnosis is uncertain or treatment has failed.

High STI risk or inconclusive symptoms — examine and investigate:

  • Inspect vulva, vagina, and cervix (speculum examination)
  • Bimanual examination if pelvic pain or PID suspected
  • Dual NAAT swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea — self-taken vulvovaginal swab is acceptable and preferred by many women; available in community in D&G
  • High vaginal swab (HVS) — consider for recurrent symptoms, failed treatment, pregnancy, or inconclusive picture; supports Amsel criteria assessment (pH, clue cells, amine test)
  • Exclude foreign body on examination
  • pH testing: BV typically pH >4.5; candidiasis pH normal (4.0–4.5)

Amsel criteria for BV diagnosis (requires ≥3 of 4):

  • Homogeneous grey-white discharge coating vaginal walls
  • Vaginal pH >4.5
  • Positive amine (whiff) test — fishy odour with 10% KOH
  • Clue cells on microscopy (>20% of epithelial cells)

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Bacterial vaginosis (BV)

Pregnancy

Avoid metronidazole 2g single dose in pregnancy. Use metronidazole 400mg BD for 5–7 days or topical metronidazole gel 0.75%. Symptomatic BV in pregnancy should be treated (associated with preterm birth and preterm premature rupture of membranes). HVS recommended to confirm diagnosis. Clindamycin vaginal cream should be avoided in the first trimester.

Acute BV — first-line treatment options

  • Metronidazole 400mg orally twice daily for 5–7 days ✓ First Choice — preferred regimen (better adherence outcomes than 2g stat; preferred in pregnancy)
  • Metronidazole 2g orally as a single dose — alternative for adherence; avoid in pregnancy
  • Tinidazole 2g orally as a single dose — alternative to metronidazole
  • Metronidazole vaginal gel 0.75% — one 5g applicator intravaginally once daily for 5 days; useful if oral not tolerated or in pregnancy
  • Clindamycin vaginal cream 2% — one 5g applicator intravaginally at night for 7 days; use if metronidazole contraindicated or not tolerated; avoid in first trimester of pregnancy

Advise: avoid alcohol during oral metronidazole and for 48 hours after; BV is not sexually transmitted but condoms may reduce recurrence; partner treatment is not routinely recommended.

Recurrent BV (≥3 episodes per year)

  • Confirm diagnosis with HVS before starting suppressive therapy
  • Treat acute episode first with standard course
  • Suppressive therapy: metronidazole vaginal gel 0.75% twice weekly for up to 16 weeks (off-licence use) — reduces recurrence in ~50% of women
  • Lactic acid gel (e.g. Relactagel) — maintains vaginal pH; evidence limited but may help between antibiotic courses; available OTC
  • Advise regarding triggers: avoid vaginal douching, perfumed soaps/products, use of shower gel internally
  • If recurrence continues despite suppressive therapy, refer to sexual health clinic or gynaecology

Vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)

Pregnancy

Avoid oral fluconazole throughout pregnancy — associated with increased risk of cardiac defects and spontaneous miscarriage (MHRA safety signal). Use topical clotrimazole pessary or cream instead. Insert pessary carefully (applicator use should be avoided in pregnancy if possible).

Acute candidiasis — first-line treatment options

  • Fluconazole 150mg orally as a single dose ✓ First Choice — preferred for convenience; avoid in pregnancy
  • Clotrimazole 500mg pessary intravaginally as a single dose ✓ First Choice — equivalent efficacy; preferred in pregnancy and where oral treatment not tolerated
  • Clotrimazole cream 2% applied to vulva twice daily for symptomatic external relief (use alongside pessary if significant vulvitis)
  • Miconazole vaginal cream or pessary — alternative topical azole if clotrimazole not available

Advise: OTC treatments are equivalent; partner treatment not routinely recommended unless symptomatic; avoid scented products, tight synthetic clothing; complete course even if menstruating.

Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC — ≥4 episodes in 12 months)

  • Confirm diagnosis with HVS (including fungal culture and speciation) — exclude non-albicans Candida (e.g. C. glabrata which may be azole-resistant)
  • Exclude predisposing factors: poorly controlled diabetes, immunosuppression, iron deficiency, antibiotic use
  • Induction phase: Fluconazole 150mg orally every 72 hours for 3 doses
  • Maintenance phase: Fluconazole 150mg orally once weekly for 6 months — reduces recurrence in ~90% during treatment; relapse common on stopping
  • If C. glabrata or non-albicans species identified, or refractory to fluconazole maintenance: refer to sexual health clinic or gynaecology
  • Advise regarding lifestyle triggers as above

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Urgent — same-day or 999

  • Suspected pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) with systemic illness — fever, rigors, peritonism, unable to tolerate oral antibiotics → same-day hospital assessment (999 if acutely unwell)
  • Suspected sepsis in a woman with pelvic/abdominal symptoms and recent gynaecological instrumentation or TOP

Mild–moderate PID can be managed in primary care with empirical antibiotics per BASHH guidance — discuss with on-call gynaecology if uncertain.

Urgent — 2-week wait (suspected cancer)

  • Post-menopausal woman with new or unexplained vaginal discharge — refer on 2ww gynaecological cancer pathway; exclude endometrial, cervical, and vaginal malignancy
  • Persistent or blood-stained discharge in any woman where cervical or endometrial pathology cannot be excluded

Sexual health clinic (Mountainhall Treatment Centre, Dumfries)

  • High STI risk requiring comprehensive STI screen and examination — especially if unable to perform in primary care
  • Positive NAAT for chlamydia or gonorrhoea requiring full STI screen, contact tracing, and specialist treatment
  • Recurrent BV not responding to standard treatment or suppressive therapy
  • Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC) not responding to fluconazole maintenance, or suspected non-albicans Candida species
  • Trichomonas vaginalis (TV) — confirmed or suspected; sexual health clinic manages contact tracing and treatment
  • Diagnostic uncertainty after examination and investigation in primary care

Gynaecology — routine referral

  • Suspected foreign body not retrievable on examination in primary care
  • Recurrent or refractory vaginal discharge despite adequate primary care management and sexual health clinic review
  • Suspected desquamative inflammatory vaginitis or other rare cause

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
• Uncomplicated BV responding to treatment — treat with standard metronidazole regimen; no referral needed
  • Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis responding to treatment — treat with fluconazole or clotrimazole; no referral needed
  • Physiological vaginal discharge — reassure; no investigation or referral needed if no red flags, normal examination (if done), and symptoms consistent with physiological variation
  • Mild recurrent candidiasis (<4 episodes/year) — manage with repeated short courses or patient-initiated treatment (woman keeps supply and treats at first symptoms); no referral needed unless predisposing cause suspected
  • BV in pregnancy responding to treatment — manage in primary care with appropriate antibiotic; refer only if symptoms persist or obstetric concern arises
  • Women requesting STI reassurance with no risk factors and characteristic BV/candidiasis symptoms — treat syndromically; no referral required
  • Positive NAAT for chlamydia in an uncomplicated case — can be managed in primary care if comfortable doing so; contact tracing can be facilitated via sexual health clinic without the woman attending in person (partner notification service available via Mountainhall)

notes_for_editor: NICE CKS URLs returned 403 — all content based on established clinical knowledge, BASHH 2012 BV guideline, and patient.info BV summary. Clinical review against current NICE CKS recommended before publishing.
Pregnancy and fluconazole: conservative position taken — avoid throughout pregnancy. Review against current SmPC and MHRA guidance (some sources restrict to first trimester only).

Recurrent BV suppressive therapy (metronidazole gel twice weekly x16 weeks) is off-licence — flag for prescribing clinician. Check D&G formulary for astodrimer gel (Betafem) as licensed alternative for RVVC prevention.
Trichomonas vaginalis included in differential table only; management deferred to sexual health clinic. Confirm this is appropriate scope for this pathway.
Lactic acid gel (Relactagel) included without BNF link — not a named BNF drug in conventional sense. Verify current BNF/MIMS status.
D&G sexual health clinic named as Mountainhall Treatment Centre, Dumfries — confirm this is still correct and that self-taken NAAT swabs remain available in community.
Clindamycin vaginal cream: listed as avoid in first trimester; check current BASHH pregnancy guidance for full trimester restriction.
